newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson image campaign seen as major flop.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson image campaign seen as major flop.

text.p: Nearly a year after O.J. Simpson was acquitted on double murder charges, image experts say his efforts to repair his battered reputation have not only flopped -- they seem to have backfired.

Simpson has courted the black community, joined a Los Angeles church and made public speeches in hopes of bridging the gap between the not-guilty verdicts returned by a 12-member jury and the view of many Americans that he got away with murder.

His acquittal in the June 1994 killings of his ex-wife and her friend has split the nation along racial lines, with opinion polls showing an overwhelming majority of whites think he's guilty while most blacks are convinced of his innocence.

But Simpson's efforts to redeem himself have failed miserably, image experts say. "I don't think it's worked at all. He is a public relations nightmare," said Los Angeles public relations consultant Dick Delson.
For his part, Simpson has given TV interviews, made regular trips to the golf course and appeared at England's prestigious Oxford University debating union.

In the process, Simpson may have dug himself into an even deeper hole by offending people who think he should have kept a low profile and by seeking to cash in on his own notoriety, image consultants said.

He finds himself dogged by protesters and hecklers when he goes out in public and is all but certain to come under even heavier fire when testimony gets under way in the wrongful-death civil case brought against him by the families of victims Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

In trying to re-establish the reputation he built as a football superstar, product endorser and sportscaster, Simpson has turned on the very people who made him a celebrity in the first place -- the news media and Hollywood.

He has blamed the press for destroying his image, and in a recent interview in Esquire magazine he said of Hollywood: "It's gotten to be a culture of whores. Everybody naming names, pointing fingers and cashing in on the gossip. Whoring used to be a profession of discretion with an implied code. Now there's no honour among thieves."

Simpson, who appeared in several Hollywood movies, including the "Naked Gun" series, "The Towering Inferno," "A Killing Affair," "Firepower" and "Goldie and the Boxer," has been spurned by the film industry since his acquittal. Car rental company Hertz dropped him as a product spokesman after his arrest, and he lost his job as a TV sports commentator.

Speaking from the pulpit at the Brookins African Methodist Episcopal Church in Los Angeles in July when he was made an honorary church member, he said, "I'm not trying to restore an image. I'm not trying to get back what wealth that I lost. I'm trying to do one thing. I'm trying to go to heaven."
But Hollywood image makers say Simpson's embracing of the black community is a case of "too little, too late."
Delson said public relations consultants from New York to Chicago and Los Angeles gave the same advice to Simpson: "Go to an island and don't come back until this all blows over."
